raw_case_text:
An 8-month old baby boy presented with high-grade fever associated with chills and rigours for 15 days, abdominal distension for 5 days and diarrhoea for 5 days. He also had an erythematous rash over his face and back. On examination, his length was 73 cm (85th percentile) and weight was 7.3 kg (3rd percentile). He was afebrile, heart rate was 140/min, respiratory rate was 38/min and blood pressure was 102/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly. No neck stiffness or signs of meningeal irritation were seen. Investigations revealed a haemoglobin of 7.2 gm/dL; total white cell count, 8300/mm3 (neutrophils, 30%; lymphocytes, 69%; eosinophils, 0%; monocytes, 1%; basophils, 0%); and platelets, 81,000/mm3. Peripheral smear for malarial parasites was negative. Tests for dengue fever were negative. Widal test revealed the antibody titers to 'O' and 'H' antigens to be 1:160 each respectively. Liver function tests showed an elevation of the hepatic enzymes - alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 94 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST), 249 IU/L; and INR, 1.3. international normalized ratio (INR) Serum creatinine was 0.4 mg/dL. Urine examination and echocardiography were both normal. Ultrasound examination of the abdomen revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly with increased echogenicity of liver. Blood culture showed S. typhi sensitive to ampicillin-sulbactam and cotrimoxazole but resistant to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins. The blood culture results were obtained on day 6 of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (14 leucocytes/mm3 with 100% lymphocytes), 38 mg/dL of proteins and 74 mg/dL of glucose. CSF Gram stain, Zeil Neilson stain and culture were negative.
The child was initially treated with IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day) for 5 days but had no response. Antibiotics were changed to IV aztreonam and oral azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day) which were given for 5 days but still the fever persisted. Hence, antibiotics were switched to IV meropenem (40 mg/kg/dose 8 hourly), and oral azithromycin was continued. The fever subsided in 13 days. IV meropenem was given for 14 days and oral azithromycin was given for 7 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-month-old infant boy presented with a 15-day history of high-grade fever with chills and rigors, a 5-day history of abdominal distension and diarrhea, and an erythematous rash over his face and back.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant developed high-grade fever accompanied by chills and rigors for 15 days, joined over the 5 days prior to admission by abdominal distension, watery diarrhea, and an erythematous rash on his face and back.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, rigors, abdominal distension, diarrhea, and facial/truncal rash.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, anthropometric measurements were length 73 cm (85th percentile) and weight 7.3 kg (3rd percentile). He was afebrile at the moment of initial exam with heart rate 140/min, respiratory rate 38/min, and blood pressure 102/74 mmHg. Cutaneous exam showed an erythematous rash over the face and back. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly. Neurological examination showed no neck stiffness or signs of meningeal irritation.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, total WBC count 8,300/mm^3 (neutrophils 30%, lymphocytes 69%, monocytes 1%, eosinophils 0%, basophils 0%), and thrombocytopenia with platelets 81,000/mm^3. Liver function tests showed elevated transaminases with ALT 94 IU/L and AST 249 IU/L, and INR 1.3; serum creatinine was 0.4 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear for malarial parasites and dengue fever tests were negative. Widal test was positive with 'O' and 'H' antigen titers of 1:160 each. Routine urinalysis and echocardiography were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly with increased hepatic echogenicity.
objective.advanced_workup: Blood culture (reported on hospital day 6) grew Salmonella typhi resistant to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins and susceptible to ampicillin-sulbactam and co-trimoxazole. Lumbar puncture/CSF analysis demonstrated lymphocytic pleocytosis (14 leukocytes/mm^3, 100% lymphocytes) with CSF protein 38 mg/dL and glucose 74 mg/dL; CSF Gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, and bacterial culture were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Extensively drug-resistant (third-generation cephalosporin- and fluoroquinolone-resistant) Salmonella typhi typhoid fever complicated by aseptic lymphocytic meningitis, hepatitis, anemia, and thrombocytopenia in an infant, confirmed by blood culture with susceptibility testing, Widal serology (O 1:160, H 1:160), and CSF examination. Malaria, dengue, and tuberculous/pyogenic meningitis were ruled out. Initial empirical IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day for 5 days) and subsequent IV aztreonam plus oral azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day for 5 days) failed to resolve the fever. Switching to intravenous meropenem (40 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 14 days) combined with oral azithromycin (continued for 7 days) achieved complete defervescence after 13 days of therapy.
